A notion is a vague, general idea or belief that exists in someone's mind — one that is often loosely held, not fully worked out, and not necessarily proven to be true.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is the quality of vagueness it carries. A notion is not a deep, carefully reasoned conclusion. It is more like a rough mental impression — something you think or believe, but haven't fully examined or confirmed.

Sense 1 — A vague idea or belief (the most common meaning)

This is the everyday use of the word. When someone has a notion about something, they have a general feeling or loose understanding of it — not a firm, certain knowledge.

Examples:

  • "She had a notion that something was wrong, but she couldn't explain why."
  • "He had no notion of how serious the situation was."
  • "I have some notion of what the job involves, but I'm not entirely sure."

Notice how in each of these, the person knows something, but it is hazy, incomplete, or unconfirmed. That fuzziness is at the heart of "notion."

Sense 2 — A sudden desire, impulse, or whim

Sometimes "notion" refers to a sudden, spontaneous urge to do something — an impulse that comes without much planning or reasoning behind it.

Examples:

  • "I had a notion to just pack my bags and travel."
  • "She took a notion to rearrange all the furniture."
  • "He woke up one morning with the notion to learn guitar."

In this sense, the notion is an unplanned, spur-of-the-moment feeling — not a well-thought-out decision.

Sense 3 — Notions (plural): small everyday items

In this specific, more narrow use — mainly in American English — notions refers to small useful items sold in a shop, typically related to sewing and clothing repair: things like buttons, needles, thread, pins, ribbons, and zippers. You might see a section in a fabric store labeled "Notions." This is a very specialized use and you will mostly encounter it in retail or sewing contexts.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Understanding how a word feels in a sentence is just as important as knowing its definition. Here is what you need to know about "notion":

It signals uncertainty or incompleteness. When you use "notion," you are indirectly telling your listener that the idea is not airtight. Saying "I have a notion that..." is softer and more humble than saying "I believe that..." or "I know that..."

It can carry a slightly old-fashioned or literary tone. You will often find "notion" in books, formal writing, and speeches. In casual everyday speech, people might instead say "idea," "feeling," or "thought." However, "notion" is absolutely used in modern everyday English — it simply has a slightly more elevated or thoughtful sound to it.

It is neutral in itself, but the surrounding words shape whether it sounds positive or negative.

  • "a beautiful notion" — sounds positive, almost poetic
  • "a dangerous notion" — sounds negative
  • "a ridiculous notion" — sounds dismissive

These words are close in meaning to "notion," but each one has a slightly different weight.

Notion vs. Idea
An idea is broader and more neutral. It can be specific, detailed, and well-formed. A notion, on the other hand, leans toward the vague and incomplete. Every notion is an idea, but not every idea is a notion.

Notion vs. Concept
A concept is a more formal, well-defined mental category — often used in academic, scientific, or professional language. A notion is looser and more personal. You might study the concept of gravity in a physics class, but you might have a notion that the weather seems to be changing.

Notion vs. Opinion
An opinion is a view or judgment you openly hold and are willing to stand behind. A notion is less committed — you might not even be ready to defend it, because it is still vague in your own mind.

Notion vs. Belief
A belief is something you hold with confidence and conviction. A notion is weaker — you suspect something or have a rough sense of it, but you are not fully certain.
Common Phrases and Patterns You Will Encounter

These are the natural combinations in which you will often see "notion" used:

  • "have a notion" — "I have a notion that things will work out."
  • "no notion of" — "She had no notion of the trouble ahead." (means she was completely unaware)
  • "some notion of" — "Do you have some notion of what you want to do?" (means a rough idea)
  • "the notion that..." — "The notion that hard work always pays off is widely believed." (introduces an idea that is then discussed or challenged)
  • "preconceived notion" — A belief you already held before encountering new information, often one that turns out to be wrong or oversimplified. "Try to let go of your preconceived notions and look at the facts."
  • "romantic notion" — An idealized, dreamy, or unrealistic idea about something. "He had romantic notions about life in the countryside."
  • "challenge/dismiss/reject the notion" — "Scientists dismissed the notion that the drug was safe."
  • "entertain a notion" — To consider or think about an idea, even if you haven't accepted it yet. "She began to entertain the notion of starting her own business."
A Summary to Lock It In

Think of a notion as an idea that lives in the early, misty stage of thought — not yet sharp, not yet proven, not yet fully formed. It's the mental sketch before the detailed painting. It can be a hazy belief you carry about the world, a sudden impulse to do something, or (in a very specific context) a small household item in a fabric store.

When you see or hear "notion," ask yourself: "Is someone expressing a loose, unconfirmed idea here?" — and the answer will almost always be yes.
